title: KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning for Generative Modelling is Designed to Mode Collapse
claim: Classical mode-seeking and mass-covering intuitions about KL hold for restrictive approximating families but break down for flexible, expressive ones.
layout: 2 panels, each a 2x3 grid of training-step plots, rows reverse vs forward KL
description: The figure has two side-by-side panels, each a 2x3 grid of small line plots. Rows are Reverse KL (top) and Forward KL (bottom). Columns are training steps, with titles such as Step 0, Step 70 or 200, and Step 600 in the left panel. A black bimodal target density, with a taller left mode and a shorter right mode, is overlaid in every plot. Panel (a), labeled 'Restrictive (Gaussian) approximation', shows a red Gaussian curve. Under reverse KL it narrows onto the left mode (mode seeking). Under forward KL it spreads broadly across both modes (mass covering). Panel (b), labeled 'Flexible (categorical) approximation', shows red histogram bars that start uniform. Under both reverse and forward KL they converge to match both modes of the target. The red-versus-black contrast draws the eye first.
caption: Illustration of how the choice of approximate distribution family affects KL optimization. With a restrictive approximate distribution (e.g. two-parameter Gaussian), KL exhibits the typical "mode seeking" and "mass covering" characteristics. This intuition does not necessarily hold for flexible distributions (e.g. independent categoricals, foundational models).
abstract: Classical intuitions cast minimizing reverse KL as "mode seeking" and forward KL as "mass covering". In KL-regularized reinforcement learning, however, the regularizer determines both the target distribution's shape and the divergence being implicitly minimized, making its role more nuanced than simply inducing generic mode-seeking or mass-covering behaviour. Specifically, the target distribution is defined jointly by the reward function, the reference model, the type of regularizer, and the regularization strength. We show that under common settings—such as low regularization strength and equal verifiable rewards—both forward and reverse KL regularization tend to specify target distributions whose mass concentrates on a single high-reward region. Thus, the objective itself by construction induces diversity collapse, regardless of the policy optimization algorithm used. Building on this perspective, we introduce a simple and scalable modification that rescales rewards to induce target distributions assigning substantial probability across all high-reward regions. This yields a principled objective that maintains high solution quality while achieving broad reward-mode coverage. Empirically, this approach improves post-training diversity and performance for Large Language Models and Chemical Language Models, and is effective with either forward or reverse KL regularization, while using either naively fails.
